extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in constitutional design, comparative government, and the history of republics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical principles for evaluating and designing stable republican constitutions drawn from historical examples (Plato, Polybius, Carthage, Rome, Sparta). Emphasizes balances of power, institutional checks, qualifications, and electoral arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of permanent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent laws are necessary to restrain the passions and vices of men, and to secure to the citizens the blessings of society, in the peaceable enjoyment of their lives, liberties, and properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that inquiry into constitutions should probe how well laws are made permanent and able to restrain private passions; examples and comparisons (Plato, Polybius) are used to show the importance of durable legal frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of different orders with opposite powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution needs different orders of men with various and opposite powers, prerogatives, and privileges to watch over one another, to balance each other, and to compel each other to be guardians of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced mixture (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) is endorsed (Polybius, Dionysius). The text repeatedly cites examples where lack of such balances led to degeneration and faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation into three harmonized divisions of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Without three divisions of power, harmonized to watch each other and compare conduct with the laws, it is impossible that the laws should at all times preserve their authority and govern all men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three orders (king/monarchy, senate/aristocracy, people/democracy) are recommended; each must act as a check on the others. Roman and Spartan arrangements are discussed as partial implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and absoluteness of each order in its department
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where three orders exist, they cannot balance each other unless each, in its department, is independent and absolute; without this independence, perpetual struggle and usurpation follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical narrative (Rome, Carthage) shows that shared executive/legislative/judicial powers or dependence of one order on another produced faction and collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive, legislative, and judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive should be separated from the legislative, and the judicial from both; ideally the king, senate, and people should each have a negative in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit design prescription: separate powers and give each branch a veto/negative to prevent dominance. The Romans' concentration of powers is cited as defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of electoral and voting mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of voting (e.g., voting by curiae vs. by centuries) fundamentally shapes constitutional outcomes; changing voting method can effectively change the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Servius Tullius' shift to centuries concentrated power in rich classes; the text warns that voting mechanics can make the poor politically insignificant despite numerical superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for membership in governing bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Public office (e.g., senators) should have qualifications such as birth, merit, and wealth; laws requiring large fortunes were used to support dignity and protect against corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off noted: wealth requirements can secure independence and resist corruption (Carthage), but risk excluding able men of humbler origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of legal/financial qualifications as anti-corruption checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring large property/fortune to be eligible for certain offices confines choice to established families and helps secure officers against bribery or venality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carthage used fortune qualifications to preserve integrity in elections and public conduct; the author notes this likely contributed to longevity of some republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalized accountability of military and executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees or councils with mandate to demand annual accounts from admirals/generals (and other officers) act as important checks on ambition and abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carthage's committee of 104 and a sub-committee of five (with life tenure and criminal jurisdiction) are offered as models: powerful but stabilizing when not made annual/elective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of making oversight bodies elective/annual
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting a small supervisory/inquisitorial body from a life, self-filling office into an annual/elective office can destroy its effectiveness and alter the constitutional balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Carthage's committee became unpopular and was made elective/annual, which the author attributes to laying the foundation for constitutional ruin by shifting balances toward popular fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal mechanisms between orders and to the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens must be able to appeal to the laws when deprived of rights; when one order encroaches, the injured should appeal to another order or to the laws to resolve disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural principle: parties should have structured avenues of appeal (aristocracy vs. democracy vs. monarchy) to preserve legal order and prevent factional violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks to prevent degeneration of one form into a worse one
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple forms of government naturally degenerate (e.g., aristocracy -> oligarchy, democracy -> tyranny); specific countervailing institutions should be put in place to prevent such degenerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptions drawn from Plato: place guardians/auxiliary bodies (e.g., a king and a democratic assembly to watch an aristocracy) to prevent slide into worse forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional plurality to prevent two-body dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to balance two assemblies effectively without a third power; where only two bodies exist, one will become predominant and seek the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carthage and Rome examples show that without a third independent order, continual scramble and eventual dominance by one body occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design trade-offs: dignity vs. inclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures (like property qualifications) intended to secure dignity and prevent corruption also risk excluding talented poorer citizens, creating a constitutional trade-off that must be weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author highlights the objection that great abilities may be possessed by men of smaller property who are thereby excluded; designers must consider exclusionary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional composition should mirror social/civic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition and powers of magistracies should reflect and reinforce national character (e.g., Carthage's commercial and military mix made commerce honorable and supported commercial genius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical observation: Carthage's combination of requirements and honors promoted commerce without effeminacy; institutional choices influence civic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware concentration of legislative, executive, and judicial powers in a single body
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating executive and judicial powers in legislative hands undermines balance and enables aristocratic dominance and factional struggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carthage and Roman examples show that when senate held most legislative and much executive/judicial authority, noble families consolidated power and the constitution destabilized.
